item.title: Air Canada fare hikes can’t keep up with soaring fuel costs, as carrier cuts forecast
item.description: Air Canada has lowered its earnings outlook by hundreds of millions of dollars for the year thanks to sky-high fuel costs after a tough quarter that saw its bottom line nearly cut in half.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: Sky-high fuel costs pushed Air Canada to slash its profit forecast by hundreds of millions of dollars for the year after a turbulent quarter that saw its bottom line nearly cut in half. The country’s largest airline recovered less than half of its fuel expanse last quarter, but aims to recoup about 70 per cent in the current one, said chief financial officer John Di Bert. The surging price of kerosene, particularly in September and after, drove a year-over-year fuel cost increase of 75 per cent or $906 million in the three months ended Sept. 30, he said. Amid an ongoing conflict in the Middle East that has throttled global oil exports, Di Bert expects the fuel price to hover around $1.72 per litre — “significantly higher than originally planned.” “That is with us for at least the foreseeable future,” he said. As a result, passengers can expect more ticket price hikes. “Fare increases remain the primary tool to offset a higher fuel environment,” he said. Airfares in Canada rose 19.4 per cent year-over-year in September, according to Statistics Canada. Air Canada lowered its 2026 financial outlook on Thursday, forecasting between $2.4 billion and $2.7 billion in earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization, versus the $2.9 billion to $3.2 billion it predicted less than three months ago. The revision comes after its net income attributable to shareholders fell 47 per cent to $139 million year-over-year in its latest quarter. However, operating revenues jumped 21 per cent to a third-quarter record of $6.98 billion, as the Montreal-based company ratcheted up airfares. The financial clouds on the near horizon relate partly to the lag between bookings and fuel prices, said chief commercial officer Mark Galardo. Air Canada has a much higher proportion of long-haul to short-haul flights than its U.S. competitors. Those longer trips are generally booked further in advance, at prices that reflect the fuel price expectations at that time. “Once those bookings are in, it’s hard to recapture (fuel costs),” Galardo noted. National Bank analyst Cameron Doerksen said that while the timeline to full cost recovery “has been pushed to the right,” complete recuperation would be possible in the first half of next year. “We believe that higher fuel costs are weighing more heavily on the profitability of Air Canada’s competitors, which ultimately will lead to more industry capacity cuts to the benefit of Air Canada,” he said in a note to investors. The sustained decline in demand for travel to the United States has pushed the carrier to scale back its cross-border service. Earlier this year, it halted or delayed eight transborder routes for the fall, then cut four more routes planned for this summer. Canadians’ return trips by air from the United States numbered 23 per cent fewer in August than the same month two years earlier, according to Statistics Canada. In the same period, Air Canada flight volumes between the two countries fell 13 per cent, figures from aviation data tracker Cirium show. However, Galardo has cautioned against reading too much into cuts to some of its cross-border corridors, noting several routes had been added as well. He said the strength of the U.S. dollar, higher profit margins south of the border and growing American demand for trips to Canada all provide tailwinds. Air Canada is also seeking to leverage the country’s location as a stopover point for Europeans and North and South Americans who cross the Atlantic Ocean. “I’ve got no reason to be concerned about the state of the transborder market,” Galardo said. Air Canada has embarked on a major expansion of its network overseas, announcing last month seven new routes in Europe and Asia for next summer. Driving the expansion are new long-range Airbus A321 single-aisle jets as well as Boeing 787 wide-bodies, though major delivery delays have hampered their rollout. The first of an expected 30 Airbus A321XLRs arrived at Air Canada in April. Six more of the fuel-efficient single-aisle aircraft  — many bound for transatlantic service — are set for delivery this quarter. Its first two 787-10s are due before the end of the year as well, on top of seven Airbus A220s — smaller narrow-bodies assembled north of Montreal — Di Bert said. The A321s jets burn 15 to 20 per cent less fuel than wide-body planes on trips across the Atlantic, he said. “This is meaningful in any environment, but it matters even more in this current fuel environment.” On an adjusted basis, the company’s adjusted earnings stayed flat at 75 cents per share last quarter, well above analysts’ predictions of 50 cents per share, according to financial markets firm LSEG Data & Analytics. This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026. Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press Companies in this story: (TSX:AC)

item.title: Canada could transition to full renewables by 2050, expert tells youth climate trial
item.description: It is “definitely” possible for Canada to transition to full renewable energy by 2050, an expert in environmental engineering and atmospheric science has told the country’s first youth-led climate ...
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: A child psychiatrist and pediatrician has described how children are disproportionately vulnerable to the effects of climate change in her testimony at Canada’s first youth-led climate trial. Dr. Elizabeth Pinsky outlined to Federal Court in Vancouver an array of risks, from susceptibility to extreme heat, air pollution and tick-borne illness to anxiety and depression linked to climate change. The Boston-based doctor pointed to several physiological factors, testifying that babies and very young children have immature thermoregulatory systems, diminishing their ability to regulate their internal temperature in a heat wave. Children breathe more rapidly than adults and take in more air pollution relative to their size, said Pinsky, an assistant professor at Harvard Medical School. There is also a “temporal reality,” she said, as younger people are “simply at increased risk” from climate hazards over the course of their lifetimes. As climate change worsens, so too will the health harms, she testified on Thursday. “There’s just no question left in the medical literature about whether that’s true.” Pinsky is a witness for 15 young plaintiffs in the trial in Federal Court in Vancouver, where they’re arguing that federal legislation violates their constitutional rights by continuing Canada’s trajectory of greenhouse gas emissions. She described the knowledge that “the people who should be protecting you and keeping you safe and safeguarding your future are not just failing to do so, but knowingly failing to do so” as a unique harm among children. The plaintiffs’ lawyer, Catherine Boies Parker, told the court in her opening statement on Monday that the case was not about the existence of climate change.  Rather, it hinges on whether the government is “constitutionally required to stop making it worse,” she said. “The plaintiffs are asking this court to hold Canada legally accountable for its role in continuing and worsening the climate crisis that is causing harm.” Pinsky also described some of the mental health effects of climate change among young people, including “eco-anxiety,” saying it can include feelings of fear, sadness, grief, anger, and a sense of betrayal and powerlessness. She explained the term “solastalgia,” meaning “the experience of feeling homesick when you are at home, but home has changed around you.” Someone might feel a sense of solastalgia when their childhood home is now engulfed in wildfire smoke every summer, Pinsky said. Nothing could fully protect children from climate harms other than ceasing to burn fossil fuels and halting climate change, she said. Pinsky is set to be cross-examined by Ottawa’s lawyers on Friday. Earlier Thursday, the court heard from Stanford University professor Mark Jacobson, an expert in environmental engineering and atmospheric science, who said it is “definitely” possible for Canada to shift to full renewable energy by 2050. He said the transition is technically and economically feasible, and the obstacles on that course are social and political in nature. Jacobson has developed sophisticated models and road maps to help cities, states and countries, including Canada, make the shift to renewable energy. Canada does not need to rely on fossil fuels, he said, outlining how the country could meet its energy demands by tapping “humongous” resources and opportunities in wind, solar and geothermal, along with pre-existing hydroelectric capacity. Combine that with the electrification of energy and transportation and “Canada can do it,” Jacobson said of transitioning to renewables by mid-century. “Whether it actually does it by 2050 is more of a social and political question.” Jacobson said electricity is significantly more efficient than combustion. “By electrifying everything and providing that electricity from renewables, you use a huge amount less energy. In Canada, it’s like 60 per cent less energy,” he said. The shift would also slash air pollution and emissions that cause global heating, he said, noting thousands of people die every year from air pollution in Canada. Jacobson agreed under cross-examination by a lawyer for the federal government that his report prepared for the trial did not present any policy proposals for Ottawa. He also acknowledged the study did not account for potential “bottlenecks” in Canada’s renewable transition, such as supply-chain constraints. Jacobson had testified earlier Thursday that his study projected a net job loss for Canada in the shift to renewables, though it wasn’t a comprehensive account. The figure excluded “the jobs that would be involved in the production of electric vehicles, electric heat pumps, other electric appliances and machines, and also some transmission distribution jobs,” he said under cross-examination. This report by Brenna Owen, The Canadian Press, was first published Oct. 29, 2026.

item.title: S&P/TSX composite finishes slightly negative, U.S. stock markets also lose ground
item.description: Canada’s main stock index edged lower on Thursday, weighed down by losses in the basic materials sector, while U.S. markets also lost ground.
item.dc:creator: The Canadian Press
item.content:encoded: TORONTO — Canada’s main stock index edged lower on Thursday, weighed down by losses in the basic materials sector, while U.S. markets also lost ground.    The S&P/TSX composite index was down 16.06 points at 36,249.03. In New York, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 132.54 points at 52,342.56. The S&P 500 index was down 23.59 points at 7,720.39, while the Nasdaq composite was down 365.13 points at 26,184.72.     The Canadian dollar traded for 71.51 cents US compared with 71.25 cents US on Wednesday. The December crude oil contract was down 78 cents US at US$102.00 per barrel. The December gold contract was down US$20.20 at US$4,031.40 an ounce.       --- This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 29, 2026.
